qs.q: An infant presents with projectile non-bilious vomiting and metabolic alkalosis due to pyloric stenosis. What is the primary renal compensatory mechanism for this acid-base disturbance?
qs.e: The kidney compensates for metabolic alkalosis by reducing hydrogen ion excretion and excreting excess bicarbonate.
qs.s: Weekly Year 2: GIT Physiology Exam - November 6, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A 3-week-old neonate presents with non-bilious projectile vomiting after feeds and a palpable, mobile, olive-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant. Laboratory testing reveals a hypokalemic, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis. What is the primary driver of the acid-base disturbance?
o: Renal retention of hydrogen ions to buffer serum
Intestinal secretion of bicarbonate due to irritation
Production of organic acids from ischemic gastric mucosa
Shift of hydrogen ions into the intracellular compartment
Gastric loss of hydrochloric acid and renal excretion
qs.e: Pyloric stenosis causes metabolic alkalosis through direct loss of gastric hydrochloric acid and paradoxical renal aciduria.
qs.s: Weekly Year 4: Paediatrics Exam - November 6, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A balanced crystalloid containing lactate is infused; the patient later develops metabolic alkalosis. Which organ primarily metabolises the lactate in this solution?
qs.e: The liver converts lactate to bicarbonate, contributing to alkalosis when large amounts are given. Kidneys play a minor role in lactate metabolism.
qs.s: Crystalloids: Types, Uses and Intravenous Fluid Therapy: MCQs

qs.q: A patient with refractory hypertension is found to have an aldosterone-secreting adrenal adenoma. Which downstream renal tubular biochemical effect accounts for the characteristic metabolic alkalosis observed in this disorder?
o: Increased apical hydrogen ion secretion with potassium wasting
Enhanced reabsorption of filtered bicarbonate in tubules
Upregulated sodium-chloride symport activity in distal tubules
Stimulation of alpha-intercalated cell proton pumps
qs.e: Aldosterone stimulates principal cells to reabsorb sodium and excrete potassium and hydrogen ions, promoting metabolic alkalosis.
qs.s: Weekly Year 2: Clinical Biochemistry Exam - October 30, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A patient presents with chronic hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis due to surreptitious diuretic abuse. Which nephron site is the primary target?
o: Early distal convoluted tubule Na-Cl cotransporter
Proximal tubule brush border Na-H exchanger
qs.e: Thiazide diuretics inhibit the Na+-Cl- cotransporter in the early distal tubule, increasing distal sodium delivery and potassium wasting.
qs.s: Weekly Year 2: Physiology Exam - October 30, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A 53-year-old man presents with persistent vomiting of undigested food eaten several days prior, accompanied by a succussion splash on physical examination and hypochloraemic alkalosis. What is the underlying mechanical problem?
qs.e: Gastric outlet obstruction presents with vomiting of old food, a succussion splash, and metabolic alkalosis due to loss of gastric acid. Afferent loop syndrome causes bilious vomiting.
qs.s: Peptic Ulcer Disease and Its Surgical Complications: MCQs

qs.q: An infant with a 48-hour history of intussusception is found to have persistent shock, metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria, and hypokalaemia. Which clinical factor is most directly responsible for the metabolic alkalosis and paradoxical aciduria?
o: Diarrhoeal loss of bicarbonate ions from the inflamed colon
Extensive fluid sequestration within the compressed vessels
Prolonged bilious vomiting leading to loss of gastric acid
Renal conservation of hydrogen ions due to dehydration
qs.e: Prolonged vomiting in intestinal obstruction leads to a loss of gastric hydrogen and chloride ions, resulting in hypokalaemic, hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria as the kidneys retain acid to excrete sodium. This is a classic electrolyte disturbance in prolonged cases.
qs.s: Intussusception in Children: Diagnosis, Air Enema and Surgery: MCQs

qs.q: A 3-week-old boy is evaluated for projectile vomiting. Laboratory results show hypochloraemia, hypokalaemia, and metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria. What is the primary renal mechanism driving paradoxical aciduria in this condition?
o: Aldosterone blockade secondary to volume depletion
The kidney excretes hydrogen ions to conserve sodium
Primary renal tubular acidosis induced by dehydration
The kidney conserves hydrogen ions over potassium
qs.e: In hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, the kidney conserves hydrogen ions at the expense of potassium, resulting in acid urine despite a systemic alkalosis. This is known as paradoxical aciduria.

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Alkalosis is a disturbance where blood pH rises above 7.45 due to excess base or loss of acid. It can be metabolic or respiratory and requires identifying the underlying cause.

sections.p: Alkalosis is defined by arterial pH >7.45. Metabolic alkalosis shows elevated HCO3⁻ with compensatory hypoventilation; respiratory alkalosis shows low PaCO₂ with renal compensation.
b: Arterial blood gas (ABG) is the cornerstone for diagnosis.
Calculate expected compensation to confirm primary disorder.

t.b: Is the pH high and what is the primary disturbance? Confirms alkalosis and distinguishes metabolic vs respiratory.
Are chloride and potassium low? Helps identify hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis.

sections.p: Severity is graded by bicarbonate level and pH: mild (pH 7.45‑7.55, HCO₃⁻ 26‑30 mmol/L), moderate (pH 7.55‑7.65, HCO₃⁻ 31‑40 mmol/L), severe (pH >7.65, HCO₃⁻ >40 mmol/L).
b: Higher severity predicts risk of arrhythmia, seizures, and respiratory failure.

sections.p: Causes are grouped by loss of acid, gain of base, or shift of H⁺ into cells.
b: Vomiting or nasogastric suction – loss of HCl (most common metabolic cause).
Diuretic therapy – volume contraction, chloride loss, and secondary aldosterone activation.
Primary hyperaldosteronism – renal H⁺ excretion and K⁺ loss.
Cystic fibrosis or chronic lung disease – chronic respiratory alkalosis.
Sepsis, malaria, severe anemia – high respiratory drive causing respiratory alkalosis.

sections.p: Patients may feel light‑headed, have tingling, muscle cramps, or seizures. Severe cases show arrhythmias, decreased ventilation, and altered mental status.
b: Hypokalaemia causes muscle weakness and cardiac ectopy.
Hypochloraemia leads to paradoxical aciduria.

sections.p: Beyond ABG, targeted tests uncover the trigger and assess complications.

t.b: Is the alkalosis chloride‑responsive? Low <20 mmol/L suggests vomiting or diuretics; >20 mmol/L suggests renal cause.
Is primary hyperaldosteronism present? Elevated ratio points to adrenal source.
Is there pulmonary disease causing chronic hyperventilation? Identifies respiratory alkalosis sources.
Use bedside capillary blood gas and clinical clues (vomiting, diuretic use) to infer alkalosis.

sections.p: Uncorrected severe alkalosis can precipitate life‑threatening events.
b: Cardiac arrhythmias (especially with hypokalaemia).
Seizures or decreased consciousness.
Respiratory depression from over‑compensation.

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then correct electrolytes and acid‑base balance.
b: Stop vomiting source; give anti‑emetics or surgical correction for obstruction.
Replace chloride (e.g., isotonic saline) to reverse volume contraction.
Correct hypokalaemia with potassium chloride; potassium repletion also helps alkalosis resolve.
Consider carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (acetazolamide) for renal‑mediated metabolic alkalosis when volume repletion fails.

sections.p: Re‑check ABG and electrolytes after 6‑12 hours of therapy. Educate patients on avoiding excess diuretics and recognizing early vomiting signs.
b: Monitor cardiac rhythm in hypokalaemic patients.
Ensure adequate oral/IV hydration before discharge.

sections.p: Conditions that present with similar symptoms or lab patterns.
b: Metabolic acidosis with compensatory respiratory alkalosis – pH may be near normal but HCO₃⁻ is low.
Hypocalcaemia – also causes tetany and seizures.

sections.p: Certain values may appear normal despite underlying alkalosis.
b: Serum chloride can be normal in mixed disorders, masking a chloride‑responsive alkalosis.
Urine pH may be high in renal tubular acidosis type 2, confusing interpretation.

whenToSeekHelp: New onset arrhythmia or cardiac arrest

faq.q: Why does vomiting cause metabolic alkalosis?
faq.a: Gastric fluid loss removes HCl, decreasing chloride and hydrogen ions, raising bicarbonate and pH.
Low K⁺ drives H⁺ into cells and stimulates renal H⁺ excretion, keeping bicarbonate high.
In renal‑mediated metabolic alkalosis when volume repletion alone does not correct the pH.

exam: Explain how to differentiate metabolic from respiratory alkalosis on an ABG and list the expected compensatory changes.
A patient with vomiting presents with pH 7.58, HCO₃⁻ 34 mmol/L, PaCO₂ 55 mmol/L. Identify the primary disorder and the most likely cause.
Describe the stepwise management of hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: Focused history and a systematic exam reveal the trigger of alkalosis and its complications while avoiding over‑interpretation of bedside signs.
b: Ask about recent vomiting, nasogastric suction, or gastric outlet obstruction; note frequency, volume and any precipitating illness.
Inquire about diuretic use, especially loop or thiazide agents; document dose, duration and adherence.
Screen for symptoms of hyperaldosteronism: hypertension, muscle cramps, polyuria, and episodes of weakness.
Ask about chronic lung disease, high‑altitude exposure or anxiety that may cause hyperventilation.
Determine pregnancy status, recent malaria or sepsis, and any HIV/TB treatment that could alter ventilation.
Review medication list for carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, steroids, or herbal diuretics.
Ask about dietary chloride intake and recent fluid losses (diarrhoea, burns).

t.b: Is the patient volume‑depleted? Look for sunken eyes, decreased skin turgor, and orthostatic tachycardia; a positive sign suggests chloride‑responsive metabolic alkalosis.
Is there a palpable olive‑shaped mass in the epigastrium? Positive in pyloric stenosis, pointing to vomiting‑induced metabolic alkalosis; absence does not rule out other causes.

t.a: Percussion for shifting dullness (if ascites suspected)
t.b: Detects free fluid; a positive test indicates volume overload, which would argue against volume‑contraction alkalosis. Bedside test cannot quantify chloride loss.

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Laboratory and bedside tests confirm the acid‑base disorder, identify the primary process and uncover the underlying trigger.
b: Arterial blood gas (ABG): pH > 7.45 confirms alkalosis; HCO₃⁻ > 30 mmol/L suggests metabolic, low PaCO₂ < 35 mmHg suggests respiratory.
Serum electrolytes: look for hypochloraemia < 98 mmol/L and hypokalaemia < 3.5 mmol/L; these support chloride‑responsive metabolic alkalosis.
Serum creatinine and urea: assess renal function; elevated creatinine may limit bicarbonate excretion and worsen alkalosis.
Urine chloride: < 20 mmol/L indicates chloride‑responsive (volume‑depleted) alkalosis; > 20 mmol/L suggests renal or saline‑responsive cause.
Urine pH: < 5.5 in the setting of metabolic alkalosis defines paradoxical aciduria, confirming renal H⁺ loss despite systemic alkalinity.
Serum aldosterone/renin ratio (if available): high ratio (> 20 ng/dL per µIU/mL) points to primary hyperaldosteronism as the cause.

t.b: If chloride < 98 mmol/L, give isotonic saline; a rise in HCO₃⁻ after volume repletion confirms chloride‑responsive alkalosis.
If urine chloride cannot be measured, use clinical volume status and response to saline challenge to infer chloride responsiveness.

sections.p: Classification integrates ABG values, electrolyte disturbances and clinical impact to guide urgency of treatment.
b: Metabolic alkalosis confirmed when pH > 7.45, HCO₃⁻ ≥ 30 mmol/L and PaCO₂ is appropriately elevated per compensation formula.
Mild severity: pH 7.45‑7.55 and HCO₃⁻ 26‑30 mmol/L; monitor, correct electrolytes, treat cause.
Moderate severity: pH 7.55‑7.60 and HCO₃⁻ 31‑38 mmol/L; requires intravenous chloride and potassium replacement, cardiac monitoring.
Severe severity: pH > 7.60 or HCO₃⁻ > 38 mmol/L; high risk of arrhythmia, seizures, respiratory depression; aggressive correction and ICU observation needed.
Volume‑contraction (chloride‑responsive) alkalosis: urine chloride < 20 mmol/L, low urine sodium, positive response to saline.
Renal (chloride‑resistant) alkalosis: urine chloride ≥ 20 mmol/L, often due to diuretics, hyperaldosteronism, or genetic tubular disorders.

sections.p: Several disorders mimic metabolic alkalosis on ABG but differ in pathophysiology and management; a focused table helps differentiate them.

t.b: Low PaCO₂ < 35 mmHg with compensatory HCO₃⁻ reduction; pH may be normal or high. Distinguish by low HCO₃⁻ and absence of hypochloraemia.
Both HCO₃⁻ > 30 mmol/L and PaCO₂ < 35 mmHg. Check expected PaCO₂; a larger drop than predicted indicates a concurrent respiratory component.
Elevated lactate with low pH; if pH is high despite high lactate, consider mixed disorder. Measure lactate and assess anion gap.

sections.p: A systematic approach prevents over‑correction and addresses the underlying cause while protecting the heart and lungs.
b: 1. Assess airway, breathing, circulation; give oxygen if SpO₂ < 94 % and consider non‑invasive ventilation for severe respiratory compensation.
2. Stop the precipitating factor – e.g., discontinue vomiting stimulus, hold diuretics, treat sepsis, or correct hyperventilation.
3. Replace volume with isotonic saline (0.9 % NaCl) to restore extracellular fluid and provide chloride, the key to reversing chloride‑responsive metabolic alkalosis.
4. Correct potassium concurrently using potassium chloride; potassium repletion also facilitates renal excretion of bicarbonate.
6. Monitor ABG, electrolytes, and urine output every 2–4 h until pH < 7.55 and HCO₃⁻ < 30 mmol/L; watch for rapid shifts that may cause hypokalaemia or hypocalcaemia.
8. Arrange definitive treatment of the underlying disease (surgical correction of obstruction, aldosterone antagonist for primary hyperaldosteronism, anti‑emetic regimen, etc.).

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Medications used to correct alkalosis have predictable adverse profiles; anticipate and mitigate them.
b: Potassium chloride – risk of hyperkalaemia if renal function declines; monitor serum K⁺ and ECG after each replacement.
Loop diuretics (if used for volume overload) – may worsen alkalosis by increasing chloride loss; give with saline and potassium supplementation.
Spironolactone (aldosterone antagonist) – hyperkalaemia risk; avoid in advanced renal failure and monitor K⁺ and creatinine.
IV bicarbonate – generally avoided in alkalosis; if given inadvertently, treat with chloride replacement and careful ventilation adjustment.

sections.p: Recognise life‑threatening sequelae early and act promptly.
b: Cardiac arrhythmias – especially torsades or ventricular ectopy with K⁺ < 3.0 mmol/L; initiate cardiac monitoring and urgent K⁺ repletion.
Seizures or altered consciousness – consider severe alkalosis (pH > 7.65) or hypocalcaemia; give calcium gluconate if ionized Ca²⁺ < 1.0 mmol/L.
Respiratory failure – rising PaCO₂ > 60 mmHg with hypoventilation; start non‑invasive ventilation or intubation.
Persistent metabolic alkalosis after correction – evaluate for hidden sources (e.g., excess bicarbonate infusion, chronic vomiting) and consider renal replacement therapy.

sections.p: Co‑morbidities can mask or modify the presentation and laboratory values of alkalosis.
b: HIV/TB – chronic lung disease may cause mixed respiratory‑metabolic alkalosis; sputum cultures and chest imaging guide therapy.
Malnutrition – low total body stores of potassium and magnesium exaggerate alkalosis; replace both electrolytes aggressively.
Pregnancy – physiologic respiratory alkalosis is normal; differentiate by checking PaCO₂ (usually 30‑32 mmHg) and avoid aggressive chloride depletion.
Diabetes mellitus – ketoacidosis treatment with insulin can swing pH; monitor glucose and bicarbonate closely.
Alcohol abuse – vomiting and diuretic use common; assess liver function as hepatic failure may blunt lactate metabolism.
Renal failure – limited ability to excrete bicarbonate; dialysis may be required for refractory alkalosis.
Age extremes – infants have limited renal concentrating ability; elderly have blunted ventilatory response; adjust monitoring frequency.

sections.p: Tailor assessment and therapy to the physiological differences of each population.
b: Children – use weight‑based fluid resuscitation; prefer oral rehydration if vomiting controlled; avoid rapid shifts that precipitate cerebral edema.
Pregnancy – give isotonic saline cautiously to avoid pulmonary edema; prefer potassium chloride over potassium gluconate to limit volume load.
Elderly – start fluid replacement slowly; watch for heart failure; use low‑dose acetazolamide if needed.
People with HIV – screen for opportunistic infections causing vomiting; consider drug interactions with antiretrovirals (e.g., acetazolamide may increase renal tubular toxicity).
Low‑resource settings – if ABG unavailable, use venous blood gas and clinical signs (dry mucous membranes, tachypnea) to estimate alkalosis; use oral rehydration salts with added chloride.

sections.p: Sample questions to test mastery of alkalosis in the contexts above.
b: 1. How do you differentiate metabolic from respiratory alkalosis on a venous blood gas?
2. A vomiting patient has pH 7.58, HCO₃⁻ 34 mmol/L, PaCO₂ 55 mmHg. Identify the primary disorder and calculate expected PaCO₂.
3. List the stepwise management of hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis.
4. Which renal tubular cell type secretes H⁺ in response to aldosterone excess and what transporter is involved?
5. Explain paradoxical aciduria and how urine pH helps confirm it.
6. In a child with pyloric stenosis, what is the main renal compensatory mechanism?
7. A patient on lactated Ringer’s develops metabolic alkalosis; which organ metabolises the lactate?
8. What are the key adverse effects of acetazolamide and how do you monitor for them?
9. When should you refer a patient with metabolic alkalosis to intensive care?
10. How does chronic liver disease alter the interpretation of a high bicarbonate level?
11. Describe how you would adjust management of metabolic alkalosis in a pregnant woman.
12. In a setting without ABG, which bedside findings most strongly suggest severe metabolic alkalosis?

facts: Metabolic alkalosis: pH >7.45 with HCO3‑ >26 mmol/L
Respiratory alkalosis: pH >7.45 with PaCO2 <35 mmHg
Hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis: urine pH <5.5 = paradoxical aciduria
Hypokalaemia (<3.5 mmol/L) predisposes to ventricular ectopy in alkalosis
Volume‑contraction alkalosis: give 0.9% NaCl to restore chloride

vivas.q: What is the primary renal compensatory mechanism in pyloric stenosis‑induced metabolic alkalosis?
vivas.a: Increased H+ secretion by alpha‑intercalated cells via H‑ATPase, driven by volume contraction and aldosterone, leading to bicarbonate reabsorption.

vivas.q: Which organ metabolises lactate in lactated Ringer’s, potentially causing metabolic alkalosis?
vivas.a: The liver converts lactate to bicarbonate via gluconeogenesis.

vivas.q: How does aldosterone excess produce metabolic alkalosis?
vivas.a: Aldosterone stimulates ENaC Na+ reabsorption and H+ secretion in alpha‑intercalated cells, causing K+ loss and bicarbonate retention.

vivas.q: Where does surreptitious diuretic abuse act to cause hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis?
vivas.a: The cortical collecting duct – inhibition of NaCl reabsorption in the distal tubule increases Na+ delivery to the collecting duct, enhancing K+ and H+ loss.

vivas.q: What mechanical problem underlies a vomiting adult with succussion splash and hypochloraemic alkalosis?
vivas.a: Gastric outlet obstruction, most often due to a pyloric or duodenal obstruction causing retained gastric contents and continuous HCl loss.

vivas.q: In intussusception‑related shock, which factor most directly causes metabolic alkalosis?
vivas.a: Severe volume depletion with chloride loss from third‑space fluid shifts, leading to renal bicarbonate retention.

vivas.q: What renal process creates paradoxical aciduria in hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis?
vivas.a: Enhanced H+ secretion by alpha‑intercalated cells despite systemic alkalosis, driven by aldosterone and low chloride, resulting in urine pH <5.5.

vivas.q: How do you differentiate metabolic from respiratory alkalosis on an ABG?
vivas.a: Metabolic alkalosis shows high HCO3‑ with PaCO2 either normal or elevated; respiratory alkalosis shows low PaCO2 with compensatory low HCO3‑.

vivas.q: A patient with vomiting has pH 7.58, HCO3‑ 34, PaCO2 55. What is the primary disorder?
vivas.a: Metabolic alkalosis with appropriate respiratory compensation (PaCO2 close to expected 0.7×(34‑24)+40 = 47 mmHg; slight over‑compensation).

vivas.q: What is the stepwise management of hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis?
vivas.a: 1) Stop vomiting source; 2) Replace chloride with isotonic saline; 3) Correct K+ with KCl; 4) Consider acetazolamide if renal‑mediated; 5) Monitor ECG and ABG.

vivas.q: Why should you avoid rapid correction of severe alkalosis with large bicarbonate loads?
vivas.a: It can precipitate hypocalcaemia, worsen intracellular acidosis, and cause volume overload.

vivas.q: What bedside history questions are essential in a patient with suspected metabolic alkalosis?
vivas.a: Onset/duration of vomiting, diuretic use, laxative abuse, volume status, medication list, and any pulmonary symptoms.

vivas.q: Which physical exam sign indicates volume depletion in alkalosis?
vivas.a: Flat neck veins and low orthostatic blood pressure suggest hypovolaemia.

vivas.q: When urine chloride is >20 mmol/L in metabolic alkalosis, what does it imply?
vivas.a: Chloride‑responsive cause (e.g., diuretics, renal tubular disorder) rather than chloride‑depletion from vomiting.

vivas.q: How does pregnancy modify the approach to metabolic alkalosis?
vivas.a: Physiologic respiratory alkalosis is normal; treat only if pH > 7.55 or symptomatic, and avoid aggressive chloride restriction.

vivas.q: What confounding factor can mask metabolic alkalosis in a diabetic ketoacidosis patient receiving insulin?
vivas.a: Insulin drives K+ into cells, causing hypokalaemia that may exaggerate alkalosis; monitor electrolytes closely.

vivas.q: Why is acetazolamide contraindicated in severe hypokalaemia?
vivas.a: It increases renal bicarbonate loss, worsening K+ depletion and can precipitate arrhythmias.

vivas.q: What is the most reliable way to confirm paradoxical aciduria?
vivas.a: Measure urine pH; a value <5.5 despite systemic alkalosis confirms paradoxical aciduria.

mcqs.q: A 2‑month‑old infant presents with projectile vomiting, palpable olive mass, serum HCO3‑ 32 mmol/L, K+ 2.8 mmol/L. Which renal change explains the alkalosis?
o: Increased distal H+ secretion via H‑ATPase
mcqs.e: Vomiting causes volume depletion and aldosterone activation, stimulating H+ secretion by alpha‑intercalated cells.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT a typical complication of severe metabolic alkalosis?
mcqs.e: Pulmonary edema is not directly caused by alkalosis; the others are recognized complications.

mcqs.q: A 45‑year‑old man with primary hyperaldosteronism has pH 7.48, HCO3‑ 28, PaCO2 48. Which tubular transporter is up‑regulated?
mcqs.e: Aldosterone increases ENaC activity, enhancing Na+ reabsorption and K+/H+ loss.

mcqs.q: In a low‑resource setting without ABG, which surrogate helps identify metabolic alkalosis?
mcqs.e: Elevated serum bicarbonate is the most direct indicator when ABG is unavailable.

mcqs.q: Which drug class is preferred to correct renal‑mediated metabolic alkalosis when volume repletion fails?
mcqs.e: Acetazolamide (a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor) promotes bicarbonate loss in the kidney.

cases.v: A 3‑week‑old boy presents with non‑bilious projectile vomiting after feeds, weight loss, and a palpable olive‑shaped mass in the right upper quadrant. Labs: Na 138 mmol/L, K 2.9 mmol/L, Cl 88 mmol/L, HCO3‑ 34 mmol/L, pH 7.55, urine chloride 12 mmol/L.

qs.q: What is the primary acid‑base disturbance?
qs.a: Metabolic alkalosis due to loss of gastric HCl.

qs.q: What renal mechanism is driving the alkalosis?
qs.a: Volume contraction activates aldosterone, increasing H+ secretion in alpha‑intercalated cells and K+ loss.

qs.q: What is the next immediate management step?
qs.a: Begin isotonic saline infusion to restore chloride and volume, then replace potassium with KCl.

cases.v: A 55‑year‑old man with refractory hypertension is found to have an adrenal adenoma secreting aldosterone. He has pH 7.48, HCO3‑ 30 mmol/L, PaCO2 48 mmHg, serum K 3.2 mmol/L, Cl 90 mmol/L. Urine chloride is 25 mmol/L.

qs.q: Explain why his metabolic alkalosis persists despite high urine chloride.
qs.a: Aldosterone directly stimulates H+ secretion via H‑ATPase in alpha‑intercalated cells, independent of chloride loss.

qs.q: Which tubular cell type is chiefly responsible for the excess H+ loss?
qs.a: Alpha‑intercalated cells of the cortical collecting duct.

qs.q: Outline the definitive treatment for his alkalosis.
qs.a: Surgical removal of the aldosterone‑producing adenoma (adrenalectomy) or targeted mineralocorticoid‑receptor blockade, followed by electrolyte correction.

mistakes: Using the wrong compensation formula for metabolic alkalosis (should be 0.7×(HCO3‑‑24)+40).
Assuming respiratory alkalosis always has low pH; compensated cases have normal pH.
Equating low urine chloride with paradoxical aciduria; urine pH <5.5 is required.
Neglecting to replace chloride before potassium, which can worsen alkalosis.
Giving bicarbonate to correct alkalosis instead of addressing the underlying cause.
Ignoring the effect of chronic lung disease on baseline PaCO2 when interpreting ABG.
